title: Pericyclic reactions I
goal: Draw the cyclic arrows of cycloadditions, electrocyclic reactions and [3,3] shifts, and say which way round and which face the partners react.

problemSets.title: The Diels–Alder reaction
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A diene and a dienophile make a six-membered ring in one step: six electrons move round a ring.
problemSets.conceptCard:
A **pericyclic** reaction has no intermediate and no ions: all the bonds change at once, with the electrons moving round a closed ring of atoms. Draw it as a loop of arrows, each one ending where the next begins; it does not matter which way round you go.

The **Diels–Alder reaction** is a [4+2] cycloaddition: a diene (four π electrons) and a dienophile (two) form a cyclohexene. Three π bonds become **two new σ bonds** and **one new π bond**, between the diene's middle carbons.

- the diene must be able to sit **s-cis**, with its ends on the same side
- it is fastest with an electron-rich diene and an electron-poor dienophile (C=C next to C=O)
- with unsymmetrical partners, the most nucleophilic end of the diene bonds to the most electrophilic end of the dienophile: a 2-substituted diene gives the *“para”* product, a 1-substituted one the *“ortho”*
- both partners react on one face (*suprafacial*), so cis groups stay cis; with a cyclic diene the C=O groups end up **endo**, under the new C=C

The app does not check stereochemistry yet: endo and exo are explained in the text.

setItems.whyThisOne: The parent reaction: three arrows round a ring of six carbons.
Unsymmetrical partners: which end bonds to which?
A fast textbook Diels–Alder, and the endo rule.

problemSets.title: Electrocyclic reactions
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: The ends of a conjugated π system join (or a ring opens), and the end groups turn in a set direction.
problemSets.conceptCard:
In an **electrocyclic reaction** one molecule closes into a ring by making a σ bond between the two ends of a conjugated π system, or a ring opens the other way. The π bonds in between shift one place along.

As the ends bond, each end carbon turns through 90°. The direction is fixed by the number of electrons involved:

- **heat, 4n + 2 electrons** (a hexatriene, 6π): **disrotatory**, the ends turn in opposite senses
- **heat, 4n electrons** (a butadiene or cyclobutene, 4π): **conrotatory**, the ends turn the same way
- under light the rules swap

So the geometry of the alkenes decides whether substituents end up cis or trans in the ring. The app checks the arrows; it cannot check cis and trans yet, so read the explanations.

setItems.whyThisOne: Six electrons close a ring: disrotatory on heating.
A strained ring opens: conrotatory on heating.

problemSets.title: [3,3]-Sigmatropic shifts
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A σ bond moves along a 1,5-diene to the far ends, through a chair-shaped ring of six atoms.
problemSets.conceptCard:
In a **sigmatropic rearrangement** a σ bond moves to a new place while the π bonds shift. In a **[3,3]** shift, number each half of the molecule from the breaking bond: the bond between the two atoms 1 breaks and a bond between the two atoms 3 forms.

- **Cope**: a hexa-1,5-diene gives another 1,5-diene; it is an equilibrium, pulled towards the more substituted alkenes
- **Claisen**: an allyl vinyl ether gives a γ,δ-unsaturated carbonyl compound; making C=O makes it irreversible
- **aromatic Claisen**: an allyl aryl ether moves its allyl group to the ortho carbon, then a proton transfer makes the ring aromatic again

The transition state is usually a **chair**, which is why the new C=C is mostly *E*. Draw these with the chain curled into a ring: the arrows are three in a loop, just like a Diels–Alder.

setItems.whyThisOne: The all-carbon [3,3] shift, driven by a more substituted alkene.
Oxygen in the chain: a C=O forms and the reaction runs one way.
A [3,3] shift that breaks aromaticity, then a tautomerisation that restores it.

problemSets.title: 1,3-Dipolar cycloadditions
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A three-atom dipole and an alkene or alkyne make a five-membered ring in one step.
problemSets.conceptCard:
A **1,3-dipole** is three atoms sharing four π electrons, drawn with charges: an azide R–N=N⁺=N⁻, a nitrone R₂C=N⁺(R)–O⁻. With the two π electrons of an alkene or alkyne (the *dipolarophile*) that makes **six electrons** moving round a ring, just like the Diels–Alder, but the ring has **five** atoms.

- the two ends of the dipole make the new σ bonds; the middle atom does not
- the charges cancel: the product is neutral
- azides and alkynes give aromatic **1,2,3-triazoles**; on heating both regioisomers form, while copper catalysis (“click”, not in the app yet) gives only the 1,4-isomer
- nitrones and alkenes give **isoxazolidines**, with oxygen bonded to the substituted alkene carbon

setItems.whyThisOne: An azide adds to an alkyne: a triazole, two ways round.
A nitrone adds to styrene: which end of the alkene meets oxygen?
